concept.name: Wyckoff Phase C
concept.definition: The third phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which price undergoes a decisive test of remaining supply (accumulation) or demand (distribution), allowing large operators to judge whether the market is ready to leave the range. Springs, shakeouts, upthrusts, and UTADs are the characteristic Phase C events.
concept.intuition: The final exam: one engineered fake move probes whether any sellers (at bottoms) or buyers (at tops) are still out there.
concept.mechanics: In accumulation, a spring or shakeout below range support tests supply; a low-volume break that quickly recovers indicates readiness for markup and offers a high-probability long entry. In distribution, an upthrust or UTAD above range resistance tests demand; its failure indicates readiness for markdown. When testing occurs higher in the range without a spring, Phase C identification is more difficult.
concept.failure_modes: The Phase C test can fail — a spring that keeps falling or an upthrust that keeps rising invalidates the range reading — and ranges without a clear test make Phase C easy to mislabel in real time.
concept.misconceptions: Phase C does not require a spring or UTAD; these are optional, and forcing the label onto every minor penetration of range boundaries is a common misreading.
concept.example: A stock dips under its six-month base on the lightest volume of the range and closes back inside it the same day (spring); the analyst declares Phase C and buys a starter position.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
citations.section: Accumulation: Wyckoff Phases (Phase C); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase C)
